entities.name: Clovis IV
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Clovis IV, often numbered Clovis III if the brief reign of Clovis III (675 CE) is discounted as a usurpation, reigned as King of the Franks from 690 or 691 CE until his premature death in 695 CE. Born in 677 CE, he was merely a child upon his accession, inheriting a crown increasingly devoid of actual power. His brief tenure epitomizes the late Merovingian period, where the nominal monarch served as little more than a figurehead, while the true authority rested with the Mayors of the Palace, particularly Pippin II of Herstal.

During Clovis IV's reign, the Frankish realm, though nominally united, was effectively governed by Pippin II, who consolidated control over Austrasia and Neustria following the Battle of Tertry in 687 CE. Clovis IV himself was a *roi fainéant*, or 'do-nothing king,' a characteristic feature of the later Merovingian monarchs who were often young, short-lived, and secluded from active governance. His primary function was to legitimate the rule of the powerful Pippinids through his royal lineage, presiding over courtly rituals while major political and military decisions were made by his powerful Mayor of the Palace.

Clovis IV's reign, though uneventful for the king himself, was profoundly significant for its contribution to the irreversible decline of the Merovingian dynasty and the concurrent rise of the Carolingian house. His status as a child king under the tutelage of an ascendant Mayor of the Palace further institutionalized the transfer of effective sovereignty, laying crucial groundwork for the eventual deposition of the Merovingians and the Carolingian usurpation of the Frankish throne. His death at a young age ensured another succession crisis, perpetuating the cycle of weak, infant rulers that the Pippinids so effectively exploited.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Clovis IV's reign, though personally uneventful due to his youth, is historically significant for illustrating the advanced decline of Merovingian royal authority and the firm consolidation of power by the Pippinid Mayors of the Palace, a critical step towards the Carolingian usurpation.
